#Q2
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
```

```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)

set.seed(8105)
```


```{r}
longitudinal_df =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$"),
    file_path = str_c("data/", file_name)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    subject_data = map(file_path, \(path) read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE))
  ) |>
  unnest(subject_data) |>
  mutate(
    subject_id = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$"),
    arm = case_when(
      str_detect(subject_id, "^con") ~ "Control",
      str_detect(subject_id, "^exp") ~ "Experimental"
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, week, outcome) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

longitudinal_df
```
```{r}
longitudinal_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject_id)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = arm), alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(color = arm), size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Outcomes by Treatment Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observed Outcome",
    color = "Treatment Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
The control group shows relatively stable outcomes over the eight weeks, with individual fluctuations but no clear overall trend. In contrast, most subjects in the experimental group exhibit increasing outcomes over time. Although there is variability between subjects in both groups, the experimental group demonstrates a clear positive trend compared with the control group.


#Q3
```{r}
# Simulate one dataset and perform a one-sample t-test
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )

  t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)

}
```

```{r}
# Run 5000 simulations for each true mean
sim_results =
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_results = map(mu, sim_t_test)
  ) |>
  unnest(test_results) |>
  mutate(
    reject_null = p.value < 0.05
  )

sim_results
```
```{r}

power_results =
  sim_results |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject_null),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

power_results
```
```{r}
power_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
Statistical power increases as the true mean moves farther away from the null value of zero. When μ = 0, the rejection proportion is approximately 0.05, consistent with the significance level. Power increases from 0.195 at μ = 1 to 0.879 at μ = 3, and approaches 1 when μ ≥ 4. With sample size and standard deviation held constant, larger effect sizes are more likely to be detected.
